contents.text: The following timeline shows events in Andrew Jackson's life on the bottom and events in U.S. history on the top. Look at the timeline. Then answer the question below.

alternativeText.text: A timeline shows events in U.S. history on one side and events in Andrew Jackson's life on the other side. In 1767, Andrew Jackson is born. From 1775-1783, the United States fights for its independence from Great Britain in the Revolutionary War. In 1781, Jackson fights in the Revolutionary War as a teenager. From 1812 through 1815, the United States fights another war against Great Britain, the War of 1812. In 1815, Jackson leads American forces to victory in the Battle of New Orleans at the end of the War of 1812. In 1818, Jackson leads a military campaign that helps the U.S. buy Florida from Spain. In 1821, the United States buys Florida from Spain. In 1824, Jackson runs for president of the United States but does not win. In 1828, Jackson is elected president.

Jackson participated in all of the U.S. history events on the timeline.

header.text: Andrew Jackson was a famous general when he decided to run for president in 1824. Jackson's military career was a major topic of discussion during the campaign. People often talked about two parts of Jackson's military record:

elements.text: In 1815, Jackson was in command of American troops defending New Orleans from the British.
In 1818, Jackson and his troops were defending Americans from a group of Native Americans, the Seminoles. They chased the Seminoles into Florida, which at that time was part of Spain's empire.

contents.text: Some Americans used these events to argue that Jackson would be a great president. Others used them as evidence that he would be a dangerous president.

contents.text: When Jackson decided to run for president, his friends and supporters thought that voters would like him more if they knew about his background. So, they wrote letters and pamphlets with facts and stories about Jackson.
For example, voters might have seen the following images of the houses Jackson lived in. Look at the images. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: Jackson's childhood home was a log cabin that is only wide enough to have one small window on either side of the front door. The roof is made of planks of wood that overlap and appear slanted.

content.text: Jackson was born in this log cabin in South Carolina. He lived in this cabin as a boy.

alternativeText.text: Jackson's adult home was a piece of land with a large white house on it. A fence sits at the front of the property, and a group of people stand outside of the fence. A winding path lined with decorative trees leads to the entrance of the house. There are tall columns supporting the roof of the house.

content.text: As an adult, Jackson became a successful lawyer and planter. He moved to this home in Tennessee.

contents.text: Jackson was popular in Tennessee, but to become president he had to win support in eastern states, too. So, his friends wrote letters about him to eastern newspapers.

The passage below is from a letter published in a newspaper in Pennsylvania in 1824, during Jackson's first presidential campaign. It tells an especially important story about something Jackson did when he was a teenager.

header.text: Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: [During the Revolutionary War,] Jackson, then only about 14 or 15 years of age, [became] a volunteer in the [military] service of his country. He was taken prisoner, when a British officer…commanded him to brush [the officer's] boots. Young as he was, he…refused to do as he was ordered, and demanded to be treated as a prisoner. The officer (and a contemptible fellow he must have been), aimed a blow at him with his sword, by which [Jackson's] hand, thrown up for defense, was [almost cut off].

meaning.text: treated fairly, as required by the laws of war

alternativeText.text: A timeline shows events in U.S. history on one side and events in Andrew Jackson's life on the other side. In 1767, Andrew Jackson is born. From 1775-1783, the United States fights for its independence from Great Britain in the Revolutionary War. In 1781, Jackson fights in the Revolutionary War as a teenager. In 1821, the United States buys Florida from Spain. In 1824, Jackson runs for president of the United States but does not win. In 1828, Jackson is elected president.

header.text: Andrew Jackson was a famous general when he decided to run for president in 1824. Jackson's military career was a major topic of discussion during the campaign. People often talked about two parts of Jackson's military record:

elements.text: In 1815, Jackson was in command of American troops defending New Orleans from the British.
In 1818, Jackson and his troops were defending Americans from a group of Native Americans, the Seminoles. They chased the Seminoles into Florida, which at that time was part of Spain's empire.

contents.text: Some Americans used these events to argue that Jackson would be a great president. Others used them as evidence that he would be a dangerous president.

Jackson's victory over the Seminoles helped the U.S. buy Florida from Spain.
While his troops controlled New Orleans, Jackson had people thrown in jail if they criticized him.
During his invasion of Florida, Jackson unjustly had two Seminole chiefs and two British citizens executed without proper trials.

contents.text: Land transportation improved in the early 1800s, but it was still cheaper and faster for goods and people to be transported over water. Unfortunately, lakes and rivers often did not connect to make convenient shipping routes. So, goods had to be unloaded from a boat on one river, loaded onto horses or wagons, taken to the next river, and loaded onto boats again. Similar steps were necessary to avoid waterfalls and rapids.

pieces.text: To make shipping more efficient, states began to dig long, shallow canals to connect lakes and rivers. The most successful was the
, constructed between 1817 and 1825. The Erie Canal connected Lake Erie to the Hudson River, which then connected to New York City.

contents.text: The Erie Canal had significant effects, in New York and beyond. Match each fact about the Erie Canal to its effect.

draggableItems.text: New York City became the nation's busiest port and its leading business center.
People around the Great Lakes could more easily buy clothes made on the East Coast.
Other states spent millions of dollars to build their own canals, hoping to make a profit as large as New York's.

Goods such as wheat could be shipped from areas near the Great Lakes, across the Erie Canal, and then down the Hudson River to New York City.
The cost of shipping products from east to west decreased sharply, so those products became cheaper for many westerners.

contents.text: When the 1800s began, the United States was a young, growing nation. Most Americans lived in states along the Atlantic Coast. Most people lived and worked on farms, and most of their tools and other products were made by hand, often at home or by local craftspeople.

header.text: But in both Europe and the United States, changes had begun that would transform people's lives. Look at the timeline to learn about some of these changes. Then answer the question below.

alternativeText.text: A timeline of transformative changes in Europe and the United States. The changes in Europe are: in 1769, an improved steam engine is built in Scotland. In 1771, the first water-powered spinning mill to make yarn is built in England. In 1783, the world's first steam-powered ship is built in France. The changes in the United States are: in 1793, the first American spinning mill to make yarn is built in Rhode Island. In 1807, the first widely successful American steamboat is built in New York. In 1811, the U.S. government begins building its first national highway. In 1821, new mills in Massachussetts spin yarn and then weave it into fabric.

contents.text: The questions that follow will deal with one of the darkest topics in the history of the United States: the enslavement of millions of people, mostly of African origin.

header.text: In North America, between the 1600s and the 1800s, European Americans established a system of slavery with rules such as these:

elements.text: Some people were allowed to own other people.
The owner of an enslaved person also owned any work done by that person.
Slaveowners could tell enslaved people what to do and punish anyone who did not obey.
Enslaved people could be bought, sold, and inherited.
When an enslaved woman had children, those children were also enslaved.

subheader.text: What was the journey like?

subpoints.text: The ship was designed to hold 454 enslaved people, but it was often overloaded, carrying as many as 740 people. To fit that many people, captains and sailors made enslaved people lie on their sides instead of their backs. Enslaved people were chained in place for most of the journey. They were brought up to the main deck for meals, but they spent most of their days lying in darkness.

as possible. Filling a ship with sailors would not make it more profitable, and cotton was not yet an important part of the system of slavery.  One ship, called the

subheader.text: What was the journey like?

subpoints.text: The ship was crowded and uncomfortable. To fit 600 or 700 enslaved people aboard, captains and sailors made people lie on their sides and squeeze together. header.text: This choice is correct:

content.text: African people are human beings, just like European people.

explanationText.text: The man in the symbol asks, "Am I not a man and a brother?" Since the symbol was created mostly for white Europeans, the man is asking Europeans to see him as a human being.

header.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: African people and European people should live separately.

explanationText.text: The symbol says nothing about whether African and European people should live together or separately.

content.text: African people should not have the same rights as European people.

explanationText.text: The symbol suggests that African people are human beings. Therefore, both groups should have the same human rights.

content.text: Many abolitionists in Great Britain had relatives who were enslaved.

explanationText.text: In the symbol, the word "brother" is a metaphor. It is not talking about individual people who are related to each other. Instead, it means that members of both groups are human beings.

contents.text: Did you know that the state of Texas was once an independent country? In the following questions, you will learn about Texas independence and how Texas became part of the United States.

The following timeline shows some important events in Texas history and United States history in the 1700s and 1800s. Events in Texas history are below the timeline. Events in U.S. history are above the timeline. Look at the timeline. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A timeline spanning from 1700 to 1850. In 1718, Spain built forts across Texas to claim the area. In 1776, the United States declared its independence from Great Britain. In 1821, Mexico, whose territory included Texas, won its independence from Spain. In 1836, Texas gained independence from Mexico and became its own country. In 1845, Texas joined the United States as the 28th state.

slave auctions. Here are a few visual signs of the artist's opinion:

subpoints.text: According to the Supreme Court, banning slavery took away slaveholders' constitutional right to own property. In this case, the property was enslaved people. Under this ruling, slavery could spread to every territory.
